Want to become an AI Engineer in 2026?

Don't start with LangChain.
Don't start with Pinecone.
Don't even start with AI Agents.
Start by understanding this roadmap. 👇

Most people jump straight into building AI apps.
They copy tutorials.
They connect APIs.
They launch chatbots.
But when something breaks...
They have no idea why.
Because they skipped the fundamentals.
Here's the AI ecosystem every aspiring AI Engineer should understand.

🧠 1. LLMs – The Brain
These power reasoning, coding, conversations, and content generation.
Examples:
• GPT
• Claude
• Gemini
• Llama 4
• Qwen 3
• DeepSeek
• Mistral
• Gemma 3
• Phi-4
👉 Learn what each model is good at and when to use it.

⚡ 2. Frameworks – The Orchestrator
Frameworks connect LLMs with tools, APIs, memory, and workflows.
Popular choices:
• LangChain
• LlamaIndex
• Haystack
• txtai
👉 These help you build production-ready AI applications.

📚 3. Vector Databases – AI Memory
LLMs don't remember your documents.
Vector databases do.
Popular options:
• Pinecone
• Chroma
• Qdrant
• Weaviate
• Milvus
• PostgreSQL (pgvector)
• Cassandra
• OpenSearch
👉 Essential for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).

📄 4. Data Extraction – Feed Your AI
Before AI can answer questions...
It needs clean, structured data.
Tools include:
• Crawl4AI
• FireCrawl
• ScrapeGraphAI
• MegaParser
• Docling
• LlamaParse
• ExtractThinker
👉 Great AI starts with great data.

🚀 5. Open LLM Access
Experiment, self-host, and deploy open-source models with:
• Hugging Face
• Ollama
• Groq
• Together AI
👉 Perfect for local development and production deployments.

🔍 6. Text Embeddings – The Search Engine
Embeddings convert text into vectors that AI can understand and retrieve.
Popular providers:
• OpenAI
• Voyage AI
• Google
• Cohere
• Nomic
• SBERT
👉 The quality of your embeddings directly impacts your RAG system.

📊 7. Evaluation – The Most Overlooked Layer
A good AI app isn't the one that looks smart.
It's the one that's measurably reliable.
Evaluate:
✅ Accuracy
✅ Hallucinations
✅ Retrieval quality
✅ Response consistency
Tools like Giskard and DeepEval help you build AI you can trust.

 If I were starting from scratch today, I'd learn in this order:
1️⃣ LLM Fundamentals
2️⃣ Prompt Engineering
3️⃣ Embeddings
4️⃣ Vector Databases
5️⃣ RAG
6️⃣ AI Frameworks
7️⃣ AI Agents
8️⃣ Evaluation
Master these, and you'll understand how modern AI systems are actually built.
Not just how to copy them.

One share could help a student, developer or job seeker understand the AI stack that companies are actually hiring for.

🚨WHY WAS COPPER GRADUALLY PHASED OUT OF MEDICINE, URBAN INFRASTRUCTURE, AND AGRICULTURE?🤯

💥Copper is one of the most powerful and oldest metals known for its antibacterial and antiviral properties. It naturally destroys bacteria, fungi, and viruses upon contact. It is also an excellent electrical and thermal conductor.

🤯Historically, copper was widely used:
- In hospitals and medical instruments
- In city water pipes (very common until the mid-20th century)
- In agriculture as a fungicide and natural crop treatment

Yet, throughout the 20th century, its use in these areas was sharply reduced in favor of synthetic materials (plastic, PVC) and patented chemical products.

Many point to the major influence of the Rockefeller family in reshaping modern medicine at the beginning of the 20th century. Through their foundations and funding, they helped steer medicine toward a predominantly pharmaceutical and chemical approach, while marginalizing natural methods and materials like copper or colloidal silver.

Today, we are rediscovering the benefits of copper (notably in hospitals to reduce nosocomial infections), but its use remains limited compared to its true potential.

Do you think the gradual elimination of copper from medicine, urban planning, and agriculture was purely a matter of cost and modernity, or do you see a deeper intent tied to the industrial and pharmaceutical interests of the last century?

Crypto Idea

What actually protected wealth past crises

A lot of people ask the same question: where should you move your money when the economy becomes unstable? Some believe in gold, others trust the U.S. dollar, and some put their faith in Bitcoin.

The reality is, there’s no universal answer. Every crisis is different, and what works in one may fail in the next.

A recent example: during the 2008 financial crisis, U.S. dollars and U.S. Treasury bonds were among the safest places to be. But in 2022, Treasury bonds fell right alongside stocks.

A lot can change in just a few years.

But there’s one thing that almost every crisis has in common 👇

During periods of extreme uncertainty, almost everything tends to fall. In March 2020, gold dropped about 15%, while Bitcoin plunged roughly 50%. Investors sold whatever they could to raise cash.

That leads to a few practical rules:

1️⃣ Keep part of your portfolio liquid.

Real estate can protect against inflation, but you can’t sell a property overnight. You need assets you can access quickly — not only to cover unexpected expenses, but also to buy quality investments after prices have dropped and the recovery begins.

2️⃣ Diversify across more than just asset classes. Diversify across countries and markets too.

U.S. stocks, international markets, crypto, gold — each behaves differently during a crisis.

And most importantly, remember this: the biggest problem during a crisis usually isn’t choosing the wrong investment. It’s being forced to sell the right one at the worst possible time. That’s why keeping part of your money in cash or different currencies across multiple accounts is an important part of any resilient strategy.

James Gunn recently hosted a screening of *Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2* and shared some fascinating behind-the-scenes insights. Here’s a curated look at the most intriguing details:

- The 1980 film Flash Gordon was a major source of visual inspiration for the director while crafting the movie’s tone and aesthetic.  
- On set, Kurt Russell repeatedly called Chris Pratt’s character “Star Wars” instead of “Star-Lord”—a flub that stuck as an ongoing joke.  
- Costume designers spent a significant amount of time perfecting Ayesha’s gown. Gunn considers it one of the most striking elements in the entire film.  
- He particularly loves the comedic chemistry between Chris Pratt and Dave Bautista, calling their dynamic effortless and electric.  
- Gunn wanted to humanize Nebula, who was originally a villain in the first film. To do that, he focused on her relationship with Gamora, framing them as sisters with a painful shared history.  
- Making the film helped Pratt process the loss of his father—an experience he found emotionally grounding.  
- The young alien girl from the Kree race? That’s Grace Gunn, James Gunn’s real-life niece.  
- Rocket’s decision to build a bomb with two buttons instead of one? It was intentional—because the device had multiple purposes.  
- Gunn praised Chris Pratt’s growth as an actor, noting his performance deepened significantly in the sequel.  
- Dave Bautista’s reaction to Ego’s “decent-sized” penis had Gunn literally falling off his chair laughing.  
- The most challenging scene to shoot was Ego’s monologue about his past. The sheer amount of exposition made it tough to keep emotionally engaging.  
- During the final battle with Ego, Pratt fell from a height of 4.5 meters, hit his head, and briefly lost consciousness—a moment that shocked the crew.  
- Kraglin’s triumphant scream at the end was inspired by Christopher Lloyd’s iconic cry in One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest.  
- One of Gunn’s all-time favorite scenes he’s ever directed? Yondu’s escape sequence—pure cinematic adrenaline.  
- He joked, “Has Baby Yoda ever killed people as brutally as Baby Groot did in the Escape Pod scene?”  
- Baby Groot antagonizes Drax throughout the film—but chooses him in the end, revealing he actually loves him the most.  
- Peter Quill’s emotional final speech over Yondu’s body was constantly interrupted by Michael Rooker’s snoring—since he was lying in the coffin.  
- Gunn confirmed that the scene featuring the remains of Ego’s children is packed with Easter eggs, some still undiscovered.  
- The fight between Gamora and Nebula was directly inspired by the plane sequence in the thriller North by Northwest.  
- Pom Klementieff was, in Gunn’s words, “born to play Mantis.” He can’t imagine anyone else in the role—and teases that her future arc will surprise us all.  
- When Rocket says, “Today I can only afford to lose one friend,” he’s referring to Yondu—because he knows Yondu plans to save Quill, at his own cost.
